World.title: Irish, Israeli soccer teams to play at neutral sites after calls to boycott the matches
World.content:
Ireland’s home game against Israel in the Nations League will be played at a neutral site and behind closed doors, the Irish soccer federation confirmed Friday.

The Football Association of Ireland, which faced calls by pro-Palestinian, anti-Israel activists for a boycott, said the October 4 game originally scheduled for Aviva Stadium in the Irish capital posed “operational challenges.”

At a recent home friendly against Qatar, Irish activists hurled tennis balls onto the pitch in protest. The balls had “Stop the Game” messages on them, referring to the Nations League matches against Israel.

The Irish federation confirmed that it received UEFA approval to move the October game. A location hasn’t been announced. The teams will also meet on September 27 at a neutral site for Israel’s “home” game.

“Following consultation with various stakeholders, the Association is of the view that operational challenges could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil, so the fixture will be played away from the Aviva Stadium,” it said in a statement.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

“The Association understands and respects the views expressed by players and staff, supporters, its members, campaigners, members of the public and the Irish footballing community in relation to this fixture.”

The federation reiterated its argument that boycotting the games could damage Ireland’s chances of qualifying for the 2028 European Championship, which Ireland is co-hosting with Britain.

Forfeiting six points “could lead to relegation to League C in the UEFA Nations League and weaken our qualifying potential for (the Euros),” it said.



Ireland is likely to qualify for Euro 2028, though, with two paths to the 24-team tournament.

The four host teams — England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales — will play in separate qualifying groups from which the top two teams in each will advance to Euro 2028. UEFA will keep two more entries for co-hosts which finish third or worse in their qualifying group.

The federation also said it has been in close contact with the Palestinian Football Association, which it said expressed its appreciation “for the principled positions taken by the Football Association of Ireland in support of the rights of the Palestinian people and Palestinian athletes.”

Ireland’s federation added that previously it had called on UEFA to suspend the Israel Football Association from UEFA competitions — in protest of Israel’s military action in Gaza. The Israel-Hamas war was sparked by the terrorist group’s attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

Neither Ireland nor Israel qualified for the 2026 World Cup.

World.title: Iran-linked group claims hack of FBI drones, threatens World Cup
World.content:
WASHINGTON — An Iran-linked hacker group claims to have breached FBI drones and has threatened to target the World Cup that kicked off this week, a monitoring group said on Friday.

The SITE Intelligence Group, an organization that monitors jihadist groups, published a statement from Handala saying they had had access “for months” to “every image and every suspect” captured by first-person view (FPV) drones used by the FBI.

The hackers said the drones featured facial recognition and license plate screening deployed for counterterrorism.

“Better tighten your World Cup security, we don’t like some of those teams at all. Don’t forget: FPVs are everywhere; you never know when one might end up right in your team’s bus,” Handala said in the statement quoted by SITE.

The FBI is deploying drones around World Cup stadiums to protect against unauthorized aircraft.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

Drone flights will be banned over US stadiums hosting matches, as well as over fan events related to the soccer tournament co-hosted by the United States, Mexico and Canada that kicked off its largest edition on Thursday.

Training for local and state police on countering unauthorized drone activity at the World Cup was part of a $500 million federal grant to combat this growing threat to sporting events.

The US Justice Department has warned of the potential for cyberattacks by Iranian actors following the US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in February that triggered the Middle East War.



Handala published photos and footage that it said were taken from the hacked drones, but SITE disputed that claim.

One video of the supposed hack was in fact produced by a software platform in December 2024 to promote a US police department’s use of its technology for surveying tornado damage, SITE said.

Handala claimed in March to have hacked the email account of FBI Director Kash Patel and published personal photos and other material online.

The US State Department has offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification of members of the group.

World.title: Tel Aviv holds first Pride parade since Oct. 7; cops impede some anti-government marchers
World.content:
Tel Aviv on Friday hosted its first Pride parade in two years, with the municipality reporting over 100,000 people in attendance after urging marchers to “vote with your feet” for more rights.

The seaside parade followed a procession of eight floats sponsored by leading corporations and staffed, respectively, by the city’s LGBTQ community center, the Tel Aviv University students’ union and six leading lines of Pride parties.

With thumping music in the background, participants danced, cooled themselves with rainbow-pattern fans, and watched as performers — most of them scantily clad, muscular men — partied on the floats.

The seventh float, organized by the PAG TLV line, featured among its dancers trans model Uri Hashin, who had on Thursday led a 250-strong anti-bullying march down Tel Aviv’s Rothschild boulevard, where a gang of boys pelted her with stones last month.

Friday’s parade was secured by some 1,000 law enforcement officers, police said.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

As the parade was getting started, police announced the arrest of a 37-year-old Haifa resident”amid concern of intent to harm participants of Pride Month events across the country,” after the unnamed man alluded in a social media post about needing to “annihilate” the “sick people.” Police said they would ask the Haifa Magistrate’s Court to extend the man’s detention.

People dance on a truck that leads the first Tel Aviv Pride parade in two years pic.twitter.com/DJLrLn0gpP — Noam Lehmann (@noamlehmann) June 12, 2026



The figure of 100,000 participants cited by the Tel Aviv municipality marked a drop from past parades, with an estimated 250,000 attending in 2019 and 150,000 turning out at the last march in June 2023, months before the Hamas-led invasion of Israel and subsequent wars.

This year’s parade went ahead despite a roughly 12-hour exchange of fire between Israel and Iran starting Sunday night. The violence, renewed after a two-month truce in the latest Iran war, caused some events in Israel to be canceled, but Friday’s parade went ahead.

Last year’s Pride event, which was scheduled for June 13, was canceled just hours in advance after Israel launched a surprise bombing campaign against Iran, triggering a 12-day war. The central Pride event in 2024 was scaled down as a sign of mourning following the October 7, 2023, atrocities eight months before.

Some marchers denied entry over anti-government material

Officers in Tel Aviv on Friday sealed off some 2.5 kilometers (1.5 miles) of coastal boardwalk from Gordon Beach, where the parade kicked off at 1 p.m., southward to the Charles Clore park, where the march ended with a large party.

Among the pop stars who performed there was 2018 Eurovision winner Neta Barzilai. On Friday, she and Nibar Znati debuted Tel Aviv’s official 2026 Pride song, “Barbura” (female swan), which recounts an ugly duckling-like story with lyrics that include “Thank you for what I am.”

People entering the boardwalk for Friday’s parade had to pass through police barricades and have their personal belongings inspected. Some people were cited in Hebrew media saying officers denied them entry for carrying anti-government paraphernalia, including protest signs and masks of government supporters known for hostility to LGBTQ people.



Footage showed officers stopping a woman because she was wearing a shirt emblazoned with an insult against National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, who oversees police.

Opposition lawmakers and LGBTQ groups slammed the officers’ conduct, noting the High Court of Justice ruled last year against a police directive barring political slogans at the Haifa Pride parade.

Police acknowledged an “isolated event” of people being inappropriately denied entry to the parade, saying they were ultimately let on to the boardwalk.

Political messaging was also visible at the boardwalk itself. A reporter for The Times of Israel saw marchers hoist masks like those that were said to be banned, as well as derogatory signs with pictures of conservative religious politicians MK Simcha Rothman and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

Another rainbow-themed sign read: “All orientations are equal, except the orientation toward fascism.”

Officers did confiscate a sign that had made its way onto the boardwalk and suggested gays could be “saved” by Jesus. An officer escorted the man holding the sign away from the boardwalk.



As the parade began, dozens of members of the Israeli Gay Youth group, as well as activists from the Pink Front protest group and the Hoshen anti-homophobia group, beat drums and chanted “democracy.”

The youth group members occasionally crouched, counted down from 10 and then jumped, chanting their slogan: “We’re here and everywhere.”

The left-leaning Democrats party also sent a contingent of activists and politicians, including MK Gilad Kariv, who thanked police for their service but warned them not to force lawmakers to make sure officers behaved appropriately.

Activists for The Democrats handed out fliers that stated, “in a Jewish democratic state everyone is equal” and said the party would ban so-called “conversion therapy,” legalize civil marriage and ensure LGBTQ families equal rights to traditional ones.

No other party appeared to have shown up in an organized manner.

Charlie Summers contributed to this report.

World.title: Trump fumes at ‘dishonorable’ Iranians amid leaks on emerging deal’s purported terms
World.content:
US President Donald Trump lashed out at Iran on Friday as the Islamic Republic and his administration leaked conflicting details to media outlets about their emerging diplomatic agreement, warning the “dishonorable” Iranians “better get their act together” after declaring the deal could be signed as soon as this weekend.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, again vowed the Iranian regime will never get its hands on nuclear weapons while asserting full alignment between himself and Trump, despite reportedly being kept in the dark about the agreement during negotiations.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said reports by Iranian state media were “Fake News,” stating they “have NOTHING to do with the terms that were agreed to, in writing,” without further specifying.

âWhat they said, including their weak and pathetic statement on having a deal, bears no relation to the truth,â Trump continued. âVery dishonorable people to deal with. With them, there is no such thing as dealing in good faith. AMAZING!â

He also said the Iranians âtotally rebuffed Drone attack last night against Indian Ships leaving the Hormuz Strait is TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE,â after the US reported downing a pair of drones targeting a commercial vessel transiting the key waterway.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

âThey better get their act together, and FAST!â Trump added, a day after calling off strikes on Iran and claiming a deal was at hand.

The US president’s post came after the official Islamic Republic News Agency reported Tehran will not give up its right to enrich uranium under any deal, while reiterating Iran has not yet made a final decision about the draft agreement. IRNA said Tehran would ânegotiate only the nuclear program solely within the framework of the Islamic Republicâs fundamental principles.â

âIssues such as Iranâs right to enrich uranium and the retention of enriched material by the Islamic Republic of Iran will be emphasized with a view to their inclusion in the final agreement,â it said.



According to Iranian state media, the draft agreement would let the Islamic Republic keep control of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global shipping route that Iran seized in the wake of the US-Israeli bombing campaign that began on February 28.

Iran, which has only allowed a trickle of ships to pass through the strait, has insisted that vessels obtain permission from its armed forces before transiting.

Quoting a source close to Iran’s negotiating team, Iran’s Mehr news agency published what it said was a text of the draft deal currently being finalized.

The draft, it said, would end the war on all fronts, including Lebanon, see the release of $24 billion in Iran’s frozen assets, and set a 60-day period for negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program.

It also includes the “suspension of sanctions on the sale” of Iran’s oil and petrochemical products, and “the complete lifting of the US naval blockade” on Iranian ports, which has been in place since April 13.

Mehr said the draft underscores the necessity for the US and its allies to pay Iran reparations for damage caused by the war and “to present reconstruction plans for Iran amounting to at least $300 billion.”



“Final negotiations will not begin before the release of half of Iran’s blocked funds, suspension of Iran’s oil sanctions and lifting of the naval blockade,” it added.

Lebanon’s Al-Akhbar newspaper, which is aligned with Iran’s Lebanese proxy Hezbollah, said the draft agreement with the US would require Israel to halt its offensive in Lebanon and give up any territory it has captured in the country’s south.

The deal includes a plan for the “rapid withdrawal” of IDF troops, the report said.

‘Satisfies all US requirements’

Rushing to perform damage control after the Iranian leaks, a senior administration official said in a statement to querying reporters that ââ nuclear material will be destroyed and removed andâ â (Iranâs) nuclear program will be dismantled.”

But those would only appear to be concessions that the US is seeking to secure from Iran during subsequent nuclear talks that the sides will hold during the 60-day truce extension inked as a result of the Memorandum of Understanding slated to be signed in the coming days.

The MOU doesnât actually see Iran make any major nuclear concessions, beyond pledging to never obtain a nuclear weapon â something Tehran has long claimed it wasnât pursuing.

The senior administration official added that the agreement will see to it that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that Iran will not provide any funding to terror groups.

The latter clause is not believed to be in the MOU and is more likely to be something that the US will try to raise during the subsequent negotiations during the 60-day ceasefire extension, though Iran is unlikely to embrace the idea.



Nonetheless, the senior administration official said in a statement, âThis is what they have agreed to. This is a performance-based deal.â

The dynamic appeared similar to what played out after the Gaza ceasefire agreement brokered by the US, which effectively divided the accord into two phases, with the first still being difficult, but thornier issues were left for later that have yet to be resolved.

In the weeks and months following the Gaza ceasefire deal, US officials insisted that Hamas had agreed to give up its weapons, something that is expected of the terror group in the second phase of the deal, and something that Hamas has shown little indication that it is prepared to do. Accordingly, Trumpâs Gaza plan has stalled.

In the case of Iran, the US is again claiming that the Islamic Republic made all sorts of major concessions up front about its nuclear program, including that the US will be allowed to extract all of Tehranâs stockpiles of highly enriched uranium, even though Tehran has made no such concession.

That issue, along with the dismantlement of Iranâs nuclear facilities, will surely be at the top of the agenda during subsequent nuclear talks, but the US appeared determined to frame these issues as already settled as it seeks to sell a deal that critics say falls well below what was promised when the war was launched.

The MOU âgoes into details on all the nuclear issues,â a senior US official insisted to the Axios news site, and âsatisfies all US requirements.â

According to that official, Trump accepted an Iranian demand that the uranium would not leave the country, but would instead be blended down inside Iran under UN supervision if a more comprehensive deal is reached.

‘Complete agreement’

Diplomats from mediating countries and from the US said the deal â to be called the Islamabad Agreement â was reached on Wednesday night in talks between Iranâs Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Qatarâs Ali Al-Thawawdi, who spoke by phone several times with Trumpâs top envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

A source with direct knowledge told Axios that Netanyahu was not updated and had to call contacts in the Trump administration to learn details of the emerging deal.



A diplomat from one of the mediating countries said to the news site that both the US and Iran have agreed on the text of the MOU, but two sources cautioned that Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has likely not approved it yet.

The MOU does not deal with the fate of Iranâs billions of dollars of frozen assets around the world, according to the report.

Speaking later, Vice President JD Vance said funds would not be released to Iran for signing the deal with the US or attending a meeting, adding that the potential agreement is structured to ensure that economic benefits would flow to Tehran if it meets its obligations.

âThe Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding has never been closer. Pending its finalization, the media should refrain from entering speculation about its content,â Araghchi tweeted Friday in a post shared by Trump. âIn line with our responsible and transparent approach, all details will be shared with the public in due course.â

Amid the conflicting accounts of the deal’s terms, Netanyahu on Friday released a statement claiming he and the US president were in complete agreement regarding the talks. The Prime Minister’s Office earlier said Jerusalem will not be bound by the deal.

“As long as I am prime minister of Israel, Iran will not have nuclear weapons,â Netanyahu pledged. âThere is complete agreement between President Trump and me on this issue.”

The statement appeared aimed at portraying a potential agreement as an achievement for Israel, or at least limiting the political damage of a deal that doesn’t address most Israeli concerns.

Also Friday, Defense Minister Israel Katz hinted that Jerusalem will have to use military force in the future to stop Iran from attaining an atomic bomb.

“Israel must ensure that, in the future as well, we retain the ability to act independently to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons,” Katz said in a statement, adding that he and the prime minister had instructed the IDF to prepare accordingly.

He said Trump was “leading efforts toward an agreement with Iran based on American interests, including the shared interest with Israel of preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.”

“We expect him to uphold this principle, as well as additional principles concerning missiles and terrorist proxies,” Katz continued, while stressing Israel will remain in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, and in the northern West Bank.

“Our security doctrine is sharp and clear. We act against both nearby and distant threats, and we strive for decisive outcomes rather than compromises and concessions,” said Katz. “A great deal is at stake during this period, and we are determined to continue leading a firm security policy that will prevent harm to our security achievements and will not endanger our ability to fight against the Shiite axis of evil led by Iran and the Sunni axis of evil led by the Muslim Brotherhood.”

US aircraft said dispatched to Europe for possible signing ceremony

With an agreement to end the war ostensibly close, four US Air Force planes were dispatched to Europe to prepare for a possible signing ceremony between the US and Iran on a deal to end the war, Axios reported Friday morning.

The planes carried equipment for Vance, who would sign on behalf of Washington in case there was a deal, the report said.

Speaking virtually to supporters of a Georgia gubernatorial candidate,” Trump said overnight, âI donât know if you heard, but we ended the war with Iran today,â according to remarks recorded by CNN.

He claimed Iran has âagreed never to have a nuclear weapon, something that we insisted on.â

Iran has disputed Trumpâs claim, with foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei saying that the Islamic Republic âhas not reached a final conclusion on the agreement.â

Israel and the US launched the war on Iran in a bid to destabilize its regime and destroy its ballistic missile and nuclear programs. Iran, whose leaders are sworn to Israel’s destruction, denies seeking nuclear arms, but has amassed uranium enriched to levels with no peaceful application.

While the fighting entered a truce on April 8, Israel and Iran exchanged fire for some 12 hours earlier this week, and the US and Iran have in recent weeks exchanged fire over the Strait of Hormuz. An unnamed US official told Reuters early Friday that US forces had shot down two one-way Iranian attack drones that appeared to target the Strait of Hormuz. The official said “traffic flow through the strait continues.”

On Tuesday, Trump accused Iran of having downed a US aircraft, and ordered strikes on Iran the following two nights. He threatened Thursday to strike again that night “very hard” and seize Iran’s oil production hub in the Strait of Hormuz.

Two US officials cited by NBC News said the US military was about three hours away from launching the strikes when Trump announced he was calling off the attack, leaving it “confused.”

The US military had already selected its targets, and the US Navy had already adjusted its operational plans and readied munitions for the strikes, NBC said.

The report added that despite Trump’s hyperbole and talk of taking Kharg, the planned strikes Thursday night would have been similar to the two previous nights and would not have targeted the island.

World.title: Iraq corruption case targets $30 million Beverly Hills mansion
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The U.S. Department of Justice has filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking to seize a Beverly Hills mansion that prosecutors say is linked to Iraqi Kurdish general Mansour Barzani and funded through what they describe as illicit financial gains.

In the filing, authorities allege that Barzani benefited from a scheme involving bribery and inflated fuel supply contracts tied to United States military operations in Iraq and Syria during the campaign against ISIS.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

Prosecutors say a contractor based in Virginia routed the funds and received hundreds of millions of dollars in federal logistics contracts.

According to the complaint, that contracting network was used to move and conceal proceeds tied to the alleged scheme.

The property at the center of the case is described in court documents as a secluded French-style villa in Beverly Hills with amenities that include a theater, a swimming pool, and landscaped gardens.

Authorities allege that the villa was purchased and improved with roughly $30 million dollars in proceeds between 2016 and 2020.

Barzani has not publicly addressed the allegations, and no criminal charges have been filed in connection with the forfeiture action at this time.

The case forms part of a wider investigation into alleged corruption involving defense contracting networks operating in the Kurdistan region, where United States forces relied heavily on local fuel and logistics supply chains during military operations against ISIS.

World.title: Ali Al-Hamadi’s road from refugee child to Iraq World Cup star
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Former Iraqi president Barham Salih and Iraqi player Ali Al-Hamadi met in a symbolic meeting highlighting two very distinct experiences defined by displacement, perseverance, and national identity.

Salih, Iraq’s president from 2018 to 2022 and now the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, sat down with Al-Hamadi as the striker prepares to represent Iraq in its first FIFA World Cup in 40 years.

The encounter was all the more meaningful for Al-Hamadi’s own narrative. The 24-year-old striker fled Iraq as a kid and grew up overseas before finally making the Iraqi national squad.

Now he is getting ready to take his country’s name to the grandest platform of all in football, a prospect that, in his early refugee years, seemed unthinkable.

Al-Hamadi now plays for AFC Wimbledon and has emerged as one of Iraq’s key offensive players in the country’s successful World Cup qualifying campaign.

The exchange between the two Iraqis showed how relocation can change lives.

Salih now heads the world’s biggest refugee organization, but Al-Hamadi’s path from refugee kid to World Cup player has become an inspiration for many Iraqis at home and abroad.

The encounter comes as Iraq prepares for their first World Cup debut since Mexico 1986, breaking a four-decade hiatus from the event.

Outside football, Al-Hamadi has also been interested in charity activities.

He is an ambassador for Beder, a charity that aims to raise awareness around mental health and suicide prevention via community activities and public engagement campaigns.

The video call highlighted a larger message about opportunity, tenacity, and what migrants can provide when they are chanced to rebuild their lives.

The encounter between a former president who has become a worldwide refugee champion and a national team striker who left the country as a youngster is a poignant reminder for Iraq of the lengthy travels that have defined many Iraqi success stories.

World.title: Iraq begin final World Cup preparations in West Virginia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The national football team of Iraq has left Chicago for White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, where it will conduct its last training camp before its 2026 FIFA World Cup campaign.

The group touched down in the country on a private plane and set up their tournament base at The Greenbrier Resort, the famous sports and training facility that will serve as their headquarters in the final phases of preparation.

The decision comes after Iraq concluded their pre-World Cup friendlies with matches against Venezuela, Spain and Andorra as coach Graham Arnold conducts last preparations for the tournament opener.

Iraq chose the Greenbrier for its high-performance training facilities, professional-level fields, and closeness to numerous World Cup host cities in the United States.

The Lions of Mesopotamia will stay at the training before heading to Boston, where they will play Norway in their debut World Cup encounter on June 16.

This is Iraq’s first World Cup since 1986 and ends a 40-year quest to return to football’s grandest stage.

Iraq, who qualified following a successful campaign and recent results such as a draw against European champions Spain, which sparked excitement among fans ahead of the event, goes into the competition.

After Norway, Iraq will play France and Senegal in Group I as the squad aims to make a mark on its long-awaited return to the World Cup.

World.title: A year after deadly Air India crash, families await answers
World.content:
Ahmedabad – Families of those killed in last year’s Air India plane crash gathered at the site on Friday to mark the anniversary of the disaster, still awaiting answers about its cause.

On June 12, 2025, a Boeing 787 crashed into a medical college shortly after take-off in India’s western city of Ahmedabad, killing 260 people in the deadliest air disaster for a decade.

Indian authorities are expected to issue an interim report in the coming days, a source of frustration to the victims’ relatives, who had been expecting a final disclosure.

Suresh Patni, a driver, came to the site where the plane exploded in a ball of flame, engulfing his teenage son Akash at his family’s tea stall.

“We are here today only to remember him on his first death anniversary,” Patni told AFP.

“He was a good student and could have done really well for himself.”

Patni commemorated Akash with a framed photograph and a life-size cutout, decorated with flowers and surrounded by scattered rose petals and lit lamps.

The crash killed 241 people on board the plane and 19 people on the ground.

Fragments of bags, clothes, and a melted shoe lie half-buried in the charred earth at the site, alongside dead trees with burned trunks.

“It pains us when we hear an aeroplane flying overhead,” Patni said, adding that their home was near the flight path of the airport in Ahmedabad, the main city in the state of Gujarat.

“Our house is still at the same location,” he said. “But we don’t feel like staying here… we are reminded of the same faces and memories.”

– ‘Important for closure’ –

Nearby, a woman wept as she embraced a framed picture of her deceased relatives, while another family scattered rose petals at the ruins of the hostel in honour of their son.

Relatives of the victims had expected a final report by Friday to explain why the disaster happened.

But with investigations continuing, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) is expected to issue only an interim report.

As required by international law, the AAIB published a preliminary report a month after the disaster.

That 15-page document said the fuel supply to the jet’s engines was cut off moments before impact, raising questions about possible pilot error.

It also published a conversation between the captain and his co-pilot about the fuel supply being cut off — two brief sentences that sparked theories of pilot suicide.

The report was met with strong criticism.

It did not say why the fuel switches were turned off — whether it was the fault of a pilot, or a result of a malfunction.

Relatives of the victims are meeting at a conference organised by lawyers, along with aviation and air safety experts in Ahmedabad.

They are due to hold a candlelight vigil after sunset.

“Why are authorities taking so much time to assess the crash?” asked Nilesh Joshi, whose wife Kaminiben Nilesh Joshi was killed, while returning home to Britain after attending a wedding in India.

“The release of the report is important for closure, for people like me who have lost their loved ones,” Joshi, who had come from London to attend the conference, told AFP.

Only one passenger survived, Briton Vishwash Kumar Ramesh, who has said he has “significant psychological scars” following the crash — in which his brother died — and “constant unanswered questions” about why it took place.

Vijay Sengal still remembers the deafening sound when the plane came down.

Sengal, a sanitation inspector at a nearby hospital, was one of the first to try to rescue the injured.

“When we tried to pick up bodies, the body wouldn’t come… instead, it was someone’s hand, someone’s leg,” he said.

He said that he, like many others, avoids the area after dark, fearing it is haunted.

“We believe in gods and also in souls,” he said. “Those passengers sitting in the plane, maybe they still have some work stuck, their last wish still unfulfilled.”

World.title: S. Korea’s ex-president gets 30 years over North Korea drone incident
World.content:
Seoul – A South Korean court sentenced ex-president Yoon Suk Yeol to 30 years in prison on Friday for sending military drones into North Korea, saying he planned the action as pretext for his disastrous martial law declaration in 2024.

The drone flights two months before Yoon suspended civilian rule, had sparked anger in Pyongyang, which accused the South of dropping propaganda leaflets as well.

Judges said Yoon intended to provoke Pyongyang “into carrying out armed or equivalent acts against South Korea’s military of people”, according to a summary of their ruling seen by AFP.

Yoon planned to “heighten inter-Korean military tensions and manufacture a national crisis” so his martial law could have been justified, they added.

The former president was given 30 years in jail over the drone incursion, a spokesperson for the Seoul Central District Court told AFP Friday.

Yoon is in detention while he appeals a life sentence for leading an insurrection with his martial law declaration.

He insists that he declared martial law “solely for the sake of the nation”.

His defence has also denied the charge over the drones, arguing that operation was in response to North Korea sending balloons carrying trash across the border that year.

On Friday, the court’s judges said the 2024 drone operation “entailed the use of South Korea’s military capabilities for private purposes”.

The judges added that powers vested in the president, including supreme command of the armed forces and the authority to declare martial law, must be exercised to protect the nation’s survival and security.

But Yoon approved the military drone operation, “believing he could arbitrarily use such powers for his own political gain,” the judges said.

– ‘Most hostile’ –

Yoon’s shock late-night national televised address in December 2024 that suspended civilian rule plunged South Korea into an unprecedented political crisis.

Martial law lasted only about six hours as lawmakers raced to the assembly building and voted it down in an emergency session.

However, it triggered protests, sent the stock market plunging and caught key allies like the United States off-guard.

Yoon is facing multiple legal cases, and Lee Jae Myung was elected president after months of political chaos in the country.

Drone flights remain a flashpoint in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.

In an incident unrelated to Yoon’s drone case, South Korean investigators found that government officials had sent drones into the nuclear-armed North in January.

President Lee expressed regret earlier this year over the incident.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s powerful sister called Lee’s statement “wise behaviour”, but hopes for a rapprochement faded after the diplomatically isolated nation returned to calling the South its “most hostile” enemy.

World.title: Asia stocks up, oil down on Mideast deal hopes
World.content:
Tokyo – Asian stocks gained and oil dipped Friday after US President Donald Trump withdrew his threat of further strikes on Iran and said a deal could be signed in the coming days.

Iran’s position remained unclear however, with foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei saying Tehran “had not reached a final conclusion on the agreement.”

Investors were also awaiting the market debut later Friday of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, set to be the biggest initial public offering in history.

Wall Street rallied and oil prices tumbled Thursday after Trump’s comments, with the broad-based S&P 500 ending up 1.8 percent.

“Donald Trump’s rhetoric flipped intraday from strike risk and hard military language toward no immediate attack, high-level diplomacy with Iran and talk of a deal being close enough to sign as soon as this weekend in Europe, with Vice President JD Vance expected to attend,” said Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

The European Central Bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 after the Iran war sent oil and gas prices soaring.

Markets see a rising chance that the Federal Reserve will also increase US interest rates. The Bank of Japan meets next week.

“(With) inflation pressures continuing to build, there will almost certainly still be a majority in favour of a (BOJ) rate hike,” said Abhijit Surya at Capital Economics.

In Asia, the Nikkei was up around 3.5 percent around midday while Seoul’s chip-heavy Kospi soared close to eight percent. The Hang Seng and Shanghai also rallied.

Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate were down around more than one percent.
